title: YOU SAID YES TO JESUS—SO WHY DO YOU KEEP LOOKING BACK?
paragraphs:
YOU SAID YES TO JESUS—SO WHY DO YOU KEEP LOOKING BACK?
Understanding Luke 9:62 — The Terrifying Mercy Behind One of Jesus’ Hardest Warnings About Following Him
There are things you left behind when you came to Jesus.
And then there are things you left behind physically...
That distinction may be where Luke 9:62 becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to your walk with Christ is not something standing in front of you trying to stop you.
Sometimes it is something behind you...
The approval of people who liked the version of you that existed before Jesus began changing you.
Maybe you stopped going there, but part of you still misses being there.
Maybe you stopped doing it, but occasionally you romanticize how it made you feel.
Maybe your hands are following Christ...
while your heart keeps turning around.
And Jesus said something about that.
Something sharp enough that we should resist the temptation to soften it.
“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”
The Greek is even worth seeing with your own eyes:
“Οὐδεὶς ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα ἐπ’ ἄροτρον καὶ βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω εὔθετός ἐστιν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ.”
Oudeis epibalōn tēn cheira ep’ arotron kai blepōn eis ta opisō euthetos estin tē basileia tou Theou.
“No one, having laid the hand upon the plow and looking toward the things behind, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say you can never remember your past.
He does not say that feeling temptation means you have already abandoned Him.
He does not say that a believer who struggles, stumbles, weeps, repents, and runs back to Christ is beyond grace.
Peter would make that impossible to believe.
So Luke 9:62 cannot honestly mean, “If you ever fail after deciding to follow Jesus, God is finished with you.”
Because if that were the meaning, who among us could stand?
Jesus is exposing the divided heart that says:
And those two words are hiding immediately before Luke 9:62.
A man had said to Jesus, in essence, “I will follow You, Lord, but first let me say goodbye to those at my home.”
At first hearing, that sounds reasonable.
Why would Jesus answer so severely?
Because this entire scene is about the cost and priority of discipleship.
Earlier in the chapter, Luke tells us that Jesus had resolutely set His course toward Jerusalem.
And while Christ has His face set forward toward the place where He will give His life for sinners, would-be disciples are surrounding Him with qualifications.
Anyone trying to plow a straight furrow while continually turning backward has a problem.
Your hands may still be holding the plow.
Your feet may technically still be in the field.
But your eyes are no longer aligned with where you are going.
Sooner or later, the line bends.
That is what makes this verse frightening.
You can look like you are moving forward while your heart is slowly curving backward.
Still have your hand somewhere near the plow...
while secretly negotiating with the life Jesus called you away from.
That old conversation is still in your phone.
That private browser history still tells another story.
That resentment still feels too precious to surrender.
That applause still matters more than obedience.
That relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ still gets defended with, “But you don't understand.”
That compromise has been renamed “just struggling” for so long that you have stopped seriously fighting it.
And somewhere beneath all the Christian vocabulary lives a sentence you would never say aloud:
This is where Luke 9:62 stops being a verse about an ancient farmer.
The Greek expression βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω—blepōn eis ta opisō—carries the straightforward picture of “looking toward the things behind.”
And εὔθετος—euthetos—means fit, suitable, well-placed for the purpose.
Jesus is speaking about fitness for the kingdom of God.
Not because salvation is purchased by flawless human concentration.
But the grace that saves us does not invite us to make peace with another master.
Jesus does not merely ask to become one cherished part of your existing life.
We often want Christianity to mean Jesus improves our life.
All gloriously true when understood biblically.
And suddenly Christianity is not merely about what Jesus can add.
It becomes about who owns everything.
Even the things you thought you had the right to keep hidden.
That is why looking backward is so serious.
Because eventually the question is not merely, “What are you looking at?”
There is an Old Testament scene hovering hauntingly near this idea.
When God judged Sodom, Lot and his family were commanded to flee.
Remember the woman who escaped physically while her gaze turned toward what God was judging.
There is a difference between remembering where grace rescued you from...
But do not romanticize your chains.
But don't decorate it in your memory until slavery starts looking like freedom.
Israel did this in the wilderness.
God delivered them from Egypt with astonishing power, yet hardship made them remember Egypt selectively.
And human hearts still do this.
We remember the pleasure but forget the emptiness afterward.
We remember the person but forget what the relationship was doing to our soul.
We remember the party but forget the morning after.
We remember the money but forget what greed was turning us into.
We remember the pornography but forget the shame, isolation, distorted desire, and secrecy.
We remember the applause but forget the exhausting prison of needing everybody's approval.
and forget that we were slaves.
Sin has a remarkable marketing department.
It resells your prison to you as nostalgia.
And perhaps someone reading this is standing in exactly that dangerous place.
You have not completely walked away from Jesus.
But you have been looking backward for a long time.
Scripture has become easier to avoid.
Things that once broke your heart barely bother you anymore.
You still love Jesus—or at least you desperately want to.
But something behind you has begun looking beautiful again.
Christ's warning is not permission for despair.
It is an alarm of mercy.
If your house were burning, love would not whisper.
Some of the hardest words Jesus ever spoke were spoken by the same Jesus who would stretch His arms across a cross for sinners.
The One warning disciples not to look back was Himself moving toward Jerusalem.
At Calvary, Jesus did what none of us could do.
This is why the answer to your backward-looking heart is not simply:
Hebrews 12 calls believers to run with endurance while fixing our eyes on Jesus.
Christian perseverance is not sustained by staring endlessly at our own determination.
The One who finished His race.
The One whose blood is sufficient for the sins you are ashamed to name.
Maybe you did more than look.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again,” and then found yourself crying over the same sin.
Maybe you feel hypocritical even reading this.
Looking back does not have to become going back forever.
The prodigal son went into the far country.
But the story did not end in the pigpen.
But Peter's story did not end beside that charcoal fire.
The thief on the cross had almost no earthly road left to walk.
Not that good people never wander.
But that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
But that Christ is worthy of getting up and following again.
But that genuine grace turns sinners back toward the Savior who purchased forgiveness with His blood.
So perhaps your prayer tonight does not need sophisticated language.
Part of me still wants what You told me to leave.
Part of me misses things that were destroying me.
Part of me wants Your kingdom and my old kingdom too.
Turn my eyes toward You again.
Because there are moments when repentance does not look dramatic.
Sometimes repentance is deleting the number.
Entering church embarrassed but determined to seek Christ again.
Sometimes repentance sounds like one trembling sentence:
There may be tears in the field.
There may be scars on the hands holding the plow.
There may be mornings when yesterday screams louder than tomorrow.
Your past can explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to become your master.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority to write your ending.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Because Christianity is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
People with histories they wished they could erase.
And grace did not pretend their sin was harmless.
Cheap religion says your sin doesn't matter.
Condemnation says your sin is all that matters.
The Gospel says your sin mattered so much that Christ died for it...
and Christ's grace is so great that your sin does not have to own you anymore.
So put your hand to the plow.
And when yesterday calls your name...
When the far country starts whispering...
When temptation says, “Just one more time”...
When shame says, “After everything you've done, you might as well go back”...
When the enemy reminds you who you were...
There is a world of difference between a disciple who falls while following Christ and a heart that has decided Christ is no longer worth following.
Do not confuse struggling with surrendering to sin.
Not because your fighting saves you.
Fight because Christ has become more precious than the chains He broke.

And if Christ has already rescued you from something you once thought you could never escape, tell part of that testimony. Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people like us.
Not because every sentence deserves remembering, but because there may come a night when your past starts sounding better than it really was.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody has their hand on the plow...
because something behind them is calling.
Don't mistake the voice of your old chains for the voice of home.
And the Savior who went all the way to the cross for sinners is still worthy of being followed all the way home.
Your past may still know your name—but it no longer gets to decide where you are going.
